title: Chatbot liability: Correct links do not cure misinformation
desc: Applies negligent-misrepresentation law to contradictory automated advice, with liability turning on reliance, loss and defences rather than error alone.

kps.k: Existing negligent-misrepresentation law can hold a business responsible for misleading chatbot advice.
kps.d: In Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149, the British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal found that Air Canada failed to take reasonable care over its chatbot’s accuracy. Air Canada denied liability for information supplied by its representatives, including the chatbot. The tribunal rejected that argument, characterising it as effectively treating the chatbot as a separate legal entity: the airline remained responsible for its website information regardless of delivery format. The decision applies an existing liability framework rather than creating a distinct category of chatbot liability.

qs.q: Moffatt does not use the words specifically, by saying they relied on Air Canada’s chatbot, I find they are alleging negligent misrepresentation.
qs.a: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Air Canada argues it cannot be held liable for information provided by one of its agents, servants, or representatives – including a chatbot.
qs.a: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: A link to the correct policy did not defeat reasonable reliance on contradictory chatbot advice.
kps.d: The chatbot offered a 90-day window to request reduced bereavement fares, while the linked webpage excluded requests after completed travel. Moffatt supplied a screenshot and submitted a timely application. The tribunal accepted that the advice influenced the purchase and rejected the suggestion that customers should cross-check different parts of the same website. The practical implication is that linking an authoritative policy does not necessarily cure misleading conversational guidance; businesses need consistency across customer-facing channels.

qs.q: They included the screenshot from the chatbot that set out the 90-day window to request a reduced rate and confirmed they had filled out the refund form and provided a death certificate.
qs.a: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: The webpage says, in part, the bereavement policy does not apply to requests for bereavement consideration after travel has been completed.
qs.a: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: The outcome depended on proof of reliance, loss and defences, not merely the existence of an error.
kps.d: The tribunal assessed documentary evidence on the balance of probabilities. Air Canada failed to supply the tariff provisions supporting its contractual defence, and its failure to produce alternative fare evidence supported an adverse inference. The tribunal awarded $650.88 in compensatory damages plus $36.14 in prejudgment interest, retaining applicable taxes and charges rather than granting the full amount requested. These findings highlight the practical importance of preserving chatbot exchanges, contractual terms and pricing evidence; they do not establish that contractual defences could never succeed.

qs.q: Moffatt, as applicant, must prove their claims on a balance of probabilities.
qs.a: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: To the extent Air Canada argues it is not liable due to certain terms or conditions of its tariff, I note it did not provide a copy of the relevant portion of the tariff.
qs.a: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: The case establishes responsibility for automated advice, not findings about generative-AI technology or error rates.
kps.d: Air Canada supplied no information establishing the chatbot’s underlying technology. The decision therefore cannot establish that a generative model produced the misinformation, measure hallucination rates or resolve liability for every form of autonomous AI. Its contribution to the debate is narrower: deploying a customer-facing automated interface did not remove the business’s ordinary responsibility for misleading representations on these facts.

qs.q: While Air Canada did not provide any information about the nature of its chatbot, generally speaking, a chatbot is an automated system that provides information to a person using a website in response to that person’s prompts and input.
qs.a: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: While a chatbot has an interactive component, it is still just a part of Air Canada’s website.
qs.a: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an: The court-and-regulator voice represented here supports the proposition directly. Applying ordinary negligent-misrepresentation principles, the tribunal treated the chatbot as part of the business’s website and held that the delivery format did not displace Air Canada’s responsibility for inaccurate information. It also found that directing the customer to a conflicting, correct policy page did not by itself defeat reasonable reliance on the chatbot. Liability was nevertheless fact-specific rather than automatic: it depended on proof of reasonable reliance and resulting loss, while Air Canada’s contractual and valuation defences failed because supporting evidence was not produced. There is no material internal variation across the supplied evidence because it concerns a single tribunal decision; its principal limitation is scope. The decision does not identify the chatbot’s underlying technology, establish a distinct AI-liability doctrine, or show that every chatbot error creates liability. As this is a curated, single-source example, it should not be treated as representative of all regulators, courts or professional bodies.

qs.q: It should be obvious to Air Canada that it is responsible for all the information on its website.
qs.a: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: It also does not explain why customers should have to double-check information found in one part of its website on another part of its website.
qs.a: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The sole source for the 2023–2024 period directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition. Moffatt v. Air Canada applies ordinary negligent-misrepresentation principles to incorrect chatbot advice rather than creating a technology-specific liability rule. It treats the chatbot as part of Air Canada’s website, holds the business responsible for information delivered through that interface, and rejects the contention that customers must resolve contradictory guidance by checking another webpage. Liability nevertheless depended on reasonable reliance, resulting loss and the failure of Air Canada’s evidentiary and contractual defences—not on the chatbot’s error alone. The source also materially limits the proposition’s technological scope: because Air Canada supplied no evidence about the chatbot’s nature, the decision does not establish that generative AI produced the misinformation or support broader conclusions about generative-model error rates. There is no cross-source internal variation to assess because this curated time-period record contains one source; its limitations narrow, but do not qualify, its support for the proposition.
